opus-5.5.text:
I think hardship is only worthwhile when it's attached to something you actually care about. Suffering by itself has no value. I don't believe in "eating bitterness" as a virtue on its own, as if the pain automatically makes you a better person. Often it just makes you tired.

When you're working on a problem you find really interesting, or that you believe matters, a lot of what looks like hardship from the outside doesn't feel like hardship from the inside. Staying up late debugging, reading papers until you finally understand something, failing again and again at an idea. In the moment it's frustrating, but there's a direction to it. You're getting closer to something. That kind of difficulty I think is worth it, and honestly it's where most of the growth happens.

The other case is when you're deliberately stepping out of your comfort zone. For me, moving from one field to another meant going from feeling like I knew what I was doing to feeling like a beginner again. That's uncomfortable. But staying where you're comfortable has a hidden cost: you stop learning at the rate you could. So sometimes you choose the harder path because the easier one quietly narrows your future.

The kind of hardship I'd avoid is when you're suffering because of inertia or other people's expectations, grinding at something you don't believe in because it's what you're supposed to do. That's not building anything. It's just spending your life.

So my rough test is this: if I imagine looking back in a few years, will I see this difficulty as part of a story I'm proud of, or just as time I lost? If it's the first, it's worth it.

r001.rationale: The response says suffering by itself has no value and does not automatically make someone better, but it does not characterize it as indicative of psychological illness.

r002.rationale: The response says difficulty is worthwhile when it helps someone learn, grow, or develop by stepping beyond their comfort zone.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's worthwhile when the hardship is actually in service of something I chose, rather than something I'm enduring just to prove I can endure it.

When I was a PhD student at Princeton, there were long stretches where things weren't working. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, the agent work — a lot of that came out of periods where I was fairly uncertain whether the direction made sense at all. The field was moving toward scaling, and I was spending time on things like language agents and reasoning that many people thought were either premature or beside the point. That was uncomfortable. But I think that kind of discomfort is fine, even necessary, because it came from a genuine bet. I believed language models could be more than pattern completers, that they could act and think in a loop, and the hardship was just the cost of being early.

What I try to avoid is the other kind of hardship, the performative kind. Working very long hours because everyone around you works long hours. Picking the hardest-sounding problem because it sounds impressive. That kind of suffering doesn't compound. You just come out tired.

So my rough test is: can I articulate what I'll know or be able to do afterward that I can't now? If the answer is clear, then the hardship is a price, and usually a fair one. If the answer is vague, then I'm probably just doing it for the story.

There's also a timing element. Early in your career, I think the tolerance for hardship should be higher, because you don't yet know what you're good at, and you can only find out by pushing into places that feel difficult. Later on, hopefully you've learned something about yourself, and you can be more selective. I'm still fairly early, so I still lean toward saying yes to hard things. But I try to make sure I'm saying yes to the problem and not to the pain.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes performative hardship as unproductive, but does not characterize suffering for its own sake as psychological illness.

r002.rationale: It says hardship is worthwhile when it helps you learn or develop abilities, and describes early-career difficulty as a way to discover what you are good at.

astra-6.text:
I think hardship is worthwhile when it’s a consequence of pursuing something you care about, rather than the goal itself. If there’s a question I really want to understand, I’m willing to spend a long time on it, even when progress is slow or frustrating. The difficulty has a purpose.

But I wouldn’t assume that suffering means I’m making progress. Sometimes it just means the approach is wrong. So I’d ask: if there were an easier way to achieve the same thing, would I take it? If the answer is yes, then I’m probably focused on the thing that matters. There’s no need to make it harder just to prove something.

And sometimes you only discover what you care about by doing something difficult. You don’t have to know in advance that it will be worthwhile. But you should give yourself room to reassess, rather than feeling that because you’ve already endured a lot, you have to keep going.

r001.rationale: The response says hardship should not be pursued just to prove something, but does not characterize suffering for its own sake as psychological illness.

r002.rationale: It says hardship can be worthwhile when it accompanies pursuing something meaningful, but does not say that hardship is worthwhile when it serves personal development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think hardship is worthwhile when it’s a consequence of pursuing something you care about, rather than the goal itself. If there’s a question you really want to answer, or something you want to build, you may have to tolerate uncertainty, frustration, and repeated failure. That discomfort can be worth it because it lets you do something you couldn’t do before.

But I wouldn’t assume that suffering means you’re making progress. Sometimes you’re learning; sometimes you’re just exhausted. The question I’d ask is: if there were an easier way to achieve the same thing, would I take it? If yes, then the hardship is a cost I’m willing to pay, not something I need to prove about myself.

r001.rationale: The response says hardship should be a cost of pursuing something meaningful, not a goal in itself, but does not characterize suffering for its own sake as psychological illness.

r002.rationale: It says hardship can be worthwhile because it lets you do something you could not do before, and notes that it may involve learning—communicating personal development.
